# nish/crypto/sha256

SHA-256 as FIPS 180-4 §6.2 defines it, in pure Nish.

```ts
import {
  SHA256_BLOCK,
  SHA256_SIZE,
  Sha256,
  sha256,
  sha256Absorbed,
} from "nish/crypto/sha256";
```

<scalar-code-group>

```ts example.ts
import { sha256, Sha256 } from "nish/crypto/sha256";

const whole: u8[] = sha256(message);

const h = new Sha256();
h.update(first, 0, toI32(first.length));
const soFar: u8[] = h.copy().digest();
h.update(second, 0, toI32(second.length));
const all: u8[] = h.digest();
```

</scalar-code-group>

<scalar-grid cols="2">

</scalar-card>

<scalar-callout type="info">

Two shapes, because they answer two different callers. `sha256(data)` is the
one-shot form for a message that is already in one buffer. `Sha256` is the
streaming form, and it exists for TLS 1.3: a handshake hashes its transcript
as the messages arrive and needs the hash of the transcript *so far* at
several points, which is what `copy()` is for — take a copy, digest the copy,
and keep feeding the original.

</scalar-callout>

Input is a window `(buf, off, len)` over a `u8[]`, so a caller hashing one
record out of a larger receive buffer does not copy it out first. A digest is
always a fresh 32-byte `u8[]`.

Every word is a `u32`, whose arithmetic is defined to wrap, so the additions
modulo 2^32 that the specification asks for are plain `+` with no masking.
Nothing here branches or indexes on the message: the only branches are on
lengths and loop counters, which a hash does not keep secret.

Every read is checked: nothing here imports `nish:unsafe`, so hashing never
makes a caller reach `unsafe`, which `--deny unsafe` refuses (the SCRAM in
`std/net/postgres.ts` is one such caller). Each read's index is instead
proven in range by the condition the loop or block it sits in runs under, so
`sha256Compress` reads a block with no bounds check at all.

Written from the specification, not ported from another implementation.

## Functions

### sha256

The SHA-256 digest of all of `data`, as a fresh 32-byte array.

An array longer than 2^31 - 1 bytes (possible under `--number-mode f64`)
is hashed whole, never cut to a prefix (`Sha256.updateAll`).

```ts
const sha256: (data: u8[]) => u8[]
```

<scalar-field name="data" type="u8[]" required>

The whole message; it is read, not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="u8[]">

A fresh 32-byte digest.

</scalar-field>

### sha256Absorbed

A fresh `Sha256` that has absorbed `a || b || c || d || e` and is not yet
finished. This is the start of a hash whose message is keyed material,
such as an HMAC's padded key block followed by its message: the parts are
absorbed in place, never joined into an array that a `push` could outgrow
and leave behind, and the caller, which owns the hasher, calls `digest`
and then wipes its `state`, `block` and `schedule`. Pass an empty array for
a part the message lacks.

```ts
const sha256Absorbed: (
  a: u8[],
  b: u8[],
  c: u8[],
  d: u8[],
  e: u8[],
) => Sha256
```

<scalar-field name="a" type="u8[]" required>

The first part of the message; it is read, not changed.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="b" type="u8[]" required>

The second part, read after `a`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="c" type="u8[]" required>

The third part, read after `b`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="d" type="u8[]" required>

The fourth part, read after `c`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="e" type="u8[]" required>

The fifth part, read after `d`.

</scalar-field>

<scalar-field name="returns" type="Sha256">

A hasher holding the five parts, ready for `digest`.

</scalar-field>

## Classes

### Sha256

A SHA-256 computation in progress: the hash value H of FIPS 180-4 §6.2 after
every whole block absorbed so far, and the bytes of the block not yet whole.

`update` may be called any number of times with windows of any length, and
the digest does not depend on where the message was split. `digest` pads the
message (§5.1.1), runs the last block or two, and ends the computation: the
padding is written into this hasher's own state, so a later `update` would
carry the padding as message, and it panics instead of answering a wrong
value. A second `digest` answers the same digest again, and a `copy` of a
finished hasher is finished too. `copy` first when the computation has to go
on.

```ts
class Sha256
```

| Member | |
| --- | --- |
| `new Sha256()` | A hasher at the start of an empty message (FIPS 180-4 §5.3.3's initial hash value). |
| `block: u8[]` | The pending bytes of the current block; the first `fill` of them are live. |
| `schedule: u32[]` | W_0 .. W_63, the message schedule of §6.2.2 step 1. It carries nothing from one block to the next and is a field only so that a long message allocates it once rather than once per block. |
| `state: u32[]` | H_0 .. H_7, the eight words of the intermediate hash value (§6.2.2 step 4). |
| `copy(): Sha256` | An independent hasher at the same point in the same message: updating or digesting either one leaves the other as it was. This is how a caller takes the hash of a prefix and keeps going. A copy of a finished hasher is finished too, and its `digest` is the same digest. |
| `digest(): u8[]` | The 32-byte message digest (FIPS 180-4 §6.2.2, the final H^(N) in big-endian order), in a fresh array. Ends the computation; a second call answers the same digest. |
| `digestInto(out: u8[], at: i32): boolean` | Writes the 32-byte message digest (FIPS 180-4 §6.2.2, the final H^(N) in big-endian order) at `out[at .. at + 32)` and ends the computation, with nothing allocated. A window outside `out` writes nothing, leaves the hasher as it was and answers `false`, rather than writing the part of the digest that fits. Once finished, the hash value is the digest, so a second `digest` or `digestInto` writes the same 32 bytes again; an `update` after it panics. |
| `update(data: u8[], off: i32, len: i32): void` | Absorbs `data[off .. off + len)`. A window outside `data` panics rather than hashing a short read, since a digest over the wrong bytes looks exactly like a digest over the right ones. |
| `updateAll(data: u8[]): void` | Absorbs all of `data`. An array of up to 2^31 - 1 bytes goes through `update`. A longer one (possible under `--number-mode f64`, where `toI32` of its length would saturate and leave a prefix) is walked with a `number` offset instead, a block at a time through `block`, so it is absorbed whole. After `digest` it panics, as `update` does. |
